title: Young Girl in a Ball Gown

image.credit: Collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A young girl in a formal ball gown, painted in oil with loose, visible brushstrokes in the Impressionist style.

source.museum: Collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page facts as supplied in the task brief (title, year, medium, Girls tag, public-domain statement); the page does not state the collection, and the page itself was not independently fetched while writing this record

context: An oil painting on canvas by Berthe Morisot, made in 1879. The source page does not state which collection holds it. It is tagged Girls, and Morisot was a woman artist who exhibited with the Impressionists.

descriptions.k: Look at the girl in her fancy party dress. A ball gown is a very special dress for a dance. The painter used soft, quick brush marks. Which part of the dress do you like best?
descriptions.g12: Berthe Morisot painted a young girl in a ball gown, a dress for a fancy dance or party. The paint looks quick and loose, and you can see the brush marks. Look at the dress and at the girl. How might she feel about wearing it?
descriptions.g35: Berthe Morisot painted this young girl in a ball gown in 1879 with oil paint on canvas. Morisot was an Impressionist, one of a group of painters known for quick, visible brushstrokes and a fresh look. Look closely at how the dress is painted. What might the brushstrokes tell you about how the painter worked?
descriptions.g68: Berthe Morisot was a woman artist who exhibited with the Impressionists, a group of painters who often used loose, visible brushstrokes to capture a moment. In this 1879 oil painting of a young girl in a ball gown, look at how the dress, the figure and the brushwork work together. What might the painter want viewers to notice about the girl and her formal clothing? Use details as evidence.
descriptions.g910: Painted in 1879, Young Girl in a Ball Gown shows a young girl in formal dress, made by Berthe Morisot, a woman artist who exhibited with the Impressionists, in the loose brushwork associated with the movement. Pictures of girls in formal clothing can suggest social expectations as well as personality. How do brushwork, color and the figure's posture shape your reading of the sitter, and what remains uncertain?
descriptions.g1112: Morisot's 1879 oil Young Girl in a Ball Gown sets a young figure in formal dress within the loose, open brushwork of Impressionism. Morisot exhibited with the Impressionists, and discussion of women artists often asks how they approached the subjects close to their own lives. How might visible brushwork loosen the formality of the dress, and what can a viewer responsibly infer about a sitter's feelings from a painted surface? Weigh the visual evidence against what is unknown.

k.daily: Look at the girl's dress. Point to the part you like best.
k.emotion: How does the girl seem to feel: happy, shy or excited? Point to what tells you.
k.observation: Find the girl's face and her dress. What else do you see?
k.analysis: Point to the girl. How much of the picture does she fill?
k.line: Trace a quick brush mark with your finger. Does it go up, down or across?
k.shape: Trace the shape of the dress in the air with your finger. What shape is it?
k.color: What colors do you see in the dress? Name your favorite.
k.texture: Imagine touching a party dress. Would it feel soft, silky or scratchy?
k.space: Point to the girl. What is behind her?
k.light: Where does the picture look brightest? Point to it.
k.meaning: Where do you think the girl is going in her party dress?
k.culture: People wear special clothes for parties. What do you wear on a special day?
k.technique: The painter used quick brush marks with oil paint. Where can you see them?
k.personal: Show how you would stand if you wore a fancy dress or suit.
k.critical: If you could ask the girl one question, what would it be?

g12.daily: Why do you think the painter chose to paint a girl in a ball gown?
g12.emotion: How might the girl feel about wearing such a fancy dress? Use the picture to explain.
g12.observation: List five things you notice about the girl, her dress and the space around her.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye land on the girl first? What helps her stand out?
g12.line: Which brush marks look quick and loose, and which look smoother?
g12.shape: What shapes do you see in the dress and in the way the girl holds herself?
g12.color: How do the colors of the dress work with the colors around it?
g12.texture: How did the painter make the dress look like cloth using only paint?
g12.space: How does the painter show where the girl is standing or sitting?
g12.light: Where does the light seem to fall on the girl? What tells you?
g12.meaning: What story could this picture tell about the girl's special day or night?
g12.culture: A ball gown is for a formal dance. How is it different from your everyday clothes?
g12.technique: Impressionist painters used brush marks you can see. Where do you see them here?
g12.personal: When have you dressed up for something special? How did it feel?
g12.critical: How would the picture feel different if the girl wore everyday clothes?

g35.daily: Which brushstrokes or colors tell you most about how Morisot wanted this picture to look?
g35.emotion: What mood does the girl's posture suggest, and how does the painting's quick, visible style add to it?
g35.observation: Describe the girl's dress from top to bottom. What do you notice about its parts?
g35.analysis: How does Morisot make the girl the main focus of the painting?
g35.line: How do the strokes and edges in the dress suggest the movement of cloth?
g35.shape: What shapes make up the girl and her gown, and how do they fit together?
g35.color: How do the colors Morisot chose for the gown and for the background work together or contrast?
g35.texture: How does the painter suggest fabric without painting every tiny detail?
g35.space: How does Morisot show the girl in relation to the space around her?
g35.light: How does light seem to fall on the dress, and what does that do for the mood?
g35.meaning: What might the girl be waiting for or thinking about? Give one idea and the evidence for it, remembering it is only an interpretation.
g35.culture: In 1879, a formal ball gown belonged to a world of dances and parties. What does the painting suggest about that world?
g35.technique: Impressionists often painted with loose, visible strokes. How does that style make this painting look different from a very smooth one?
g35.personal: How do clothes change the way you feel or act? Connect your answer to the girl in the painting.
g35.critical: How can we tell what the girl is really feeling from a painting? What can we not know?

g68.daily: How does Morisot's loose brushwork change the way you read a formal subject like a ball gown?
g68.emotion: How might the girl's posture and the open brushwork work together to suggest her mood?
g68.observation: Compare how the dress, the girl's face and the background are painted. Where is the brushwork most loose, and where most careful?
g68.analysis: How does Morisot organize the figure and the gown so that the viewer's eye moves through the painting?
g68.line: How do the direction and energy of the brushstrokes create a sense of movement in the figure and gown?
g68.shape: How does the overall silhouette of the girl in her gown balance with the space around her?
g68.color: How do color relationships in the gown and the background create harmony or contrast?
g68.texture: How does Morisot suggest the feel of formal fabric through brushwork rather than fine detail?
g68.space: How does the painter place the figure in space, and how much of the setting is spelled out?
g68.light: How do light and shadow, as suggested by the paint, shape the figure and the gown?
g68.meaning: What might a young girl in formal dress represent: childhood, growing up or social expectation? Support your idea with visual evidence.
g68.culture: Morisot was a woman who exhibited with the Impressionists. What might that tell you about her place in the art world of her time?
g68.technique: How does loose, visible brushwork capture a moment differently from a carefully blended surface?
g68.personal: How do special clothes make you act, stand or feel differently, and how might that be shown here?
g68.critical: Is the girl's dress or the girl herself the real subject? Make an argument using what you see.

g910.daily: How does Morisot balance a formal subject with informal, open handling of paint?
g910.emotion: What emotional register do posture and brushwork establish, and how provisional is that reading?
g910.observation: Examine places where brushstrokes are most visible. What do they reveal about how Morisot built the image?
g910.analysis: How does the composition place emphasis on the figure over the gown, or on the gown over the figure?
g910.line: How do brushstrokes act as line, defining contour and suggesting movement without a strict outline?
g910.shape: How do the broad forms of the gown and the figure shape the overall design of the canvas?
g910.color: How do color relationships unify the figure and her surroundings in an Impressionist manner?
g910.texture: How does brushwork evoke fabric and surface while keeping the paint itself visible?
g910.space: How does the handling of the setting keep attention on the figure, and what does it suggest about her environment?
g910.light: How does the painting suggest light through color and stroke?
g910.meaning: A young sitter in formal dress can suggest social expectation as well as individuality. Which visual evidence supports either reading?
g910.culture: Morisot was a woman artist exhibiting with the Impressionists. How might that context shape how we read this work, and how might it mislead us?
g910.technique: How does Impressionist technique favor the impression of a moment over detailed finish, and where do you see that here?
g910.personal: How do clothes and expectations shape how you present yourself, and how might the sitter have felt something similar?
g910.critical: What can a painted surface honestly tell us about a sitter's feelings, and what must remain interpretation?

g1112.daily: How does the tension between formal clothing and informal brushwork animate this painting?
g1112.emotion: What responsibility does a viewer have when reading a young sitter's feelings from a painted image?
g1112.observation: What does close attention to the edges where gown meets surroundings reveal about Morisot's priorities?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition construct the sitter as an individual, a social type or both?
g1112.line: How does Morisot's stroke function simultaneously as description and as mark-making?
g1112.shape: How do the large masses of the gown and the figure interact with the surrounding space to produce structure from loosely handled paint?
g1112.color: How do the color harmonies unify the canvas, and what do they suggest about Impressionist interest in perception?
g1112.texture: How does the visible handling of paint call attention to the painting as an object as well as an image?
g1112.space: How might the economy of the setting direct attention to the sitter, and what does it leave unsaid?
g1112.light: How might Morisot translate the effects of light on fabric into patches of color, and what is gained by doing so?
g1112.meaning: How might the picture's treatment of a girl in formal dress address childhood and social expectation, and how would you test that reading?
g1112.culture: How might Morisot's position as a woman exhibiting with the Impressionists inform how she and her contemporaries approached subjects such as young sitters and formal dress?
g1112.technique: How does loose brushwork redefine what counts as a finished picture?
g1112.personal: How do your own experiences of formal occasions shape what you project onto the sitter?
g1112.critical: How do biographical facts about an artist, such as being a woman in the Impressionist group, help or limit the interpretation of a single painting?

teacherNote.context: An 1879 oil painting by Berthe Morisot, a woman artist who exhibited with the Impressionists. The source page does not say which collection holds the painting, so check the holding institution before citing it. The text here sticks to what the title, medium and year support.
directions: Have students describe the girl's dress using only what they can see, then list what they cannot know, such as her name or her thoughts.
Ask students to try the Impressionist approach: paint or draw a figure in clothing using quick, visible strokes and no outlines.
With older students, discuss how much a painted surface can tell us about a sitter's feelings, and how Morisot's role among the Impressionists may shape the way the painting is discussed.
